picks.title: Claude's new Scarlet Letter watermark is invisible—for now
picks.excerpt: Anthropic's new text watermark flags anything Claude touched, including human writing the model only edited. For writers and editors that turns light AI assistance into a permanently detectable mark on the manuscript.
picks.rationale: The AI-disclosure argument stops being voluntary the moment the model marks the file itself — every author who lets Claude near a draft needs to know that today.

picks.title: After Editing Two AI-Assisted Manuscripts, I Rewrote My Client Agreement
picks.excerpt: A freelance editor describes what AI-assisted manuscripts actually look like on the page and why they cost more to fix. She rewrote her client agreement to add AI-disclosure terms and a surcharge for heavily generated drafts.
picks.rationale: The rarest kind of AI story: not a position paper but contract language and a price, written by someone who had to fix the pages.

picks.title: News Summary: AI-Generated Stories Outperform Human Writing in Reader Ratings
picks.excerpt: A Villanova University study finds readers largely cannot tell AI-generated short fiction from human-written work, and often rate the AI stories higher. ALLi unpacks what that means for indie authors' disclosure and craft decisions.
picks.rationale: Peer-reviewed evidence that the 'readers will always know' defence does not hold, which forces disclosure and positioning to carry the weight instead of quality alone.

picks.title: Reading Between the Lines, Part 2: Cognitive Debt and the Adaptive Publisher
picks.excerpt: The central risk of AI in publishing is framed not as hallucination but as "cognitive debt" — the gradual erosion of the human judgement that gives writing its originality and integrity. Part 2 sets out how an adaptive publisher should design workflows to pay that debt down.
picks.rationale: Reframes the risk from output errors to eroded judgement and then names the workflow checkpoints that pay it back — a usable editorial design, not another warning.

picks.title: The web's newest weapon against AI scrapers is a font
picks.excerpt: "ShieldFont" scrambles text for AI training crawlers while staying perfectly readable to humans. It's a typographic defence writers and publishers can apply to serialized fiction, samples, and newsletter archives.
picks.rationale: A defence an author or small press can actually deploy this week — protection that lives in the typeface rather than in a licensing negotiation nobody has leverage in.
